newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan FTC unveils guidelines for holding firms.
newsitem.headline: Japan FTC unveils guidelines for holding firms.

text.p: Japan's anti-monopoly watchdog said on Wednesday that draft guidelines for lifting a ban on holding companies will define a big financial institution as one with assets of more than 15 trillion yen.
The Fair Trade Commission (FTC) also plans to allow financial institutions to own more than five percent of shares in any other financial institution, an FTC official said.
At present, Japanese financial institutions are banned from owning more than five percent of shares in other companies and financial institutions.
In June, parliament revised Japan's anti-monopoly law to lift a ban on holding companies imposed by U.S. Occupation forces after World War Two. The revision will take effect by mid-December.
Holding companies are firms which control one or more other firms, often by holding a majority stake in them, but do not themselves engage in a specific business.
Under the revised law, the watchdog said three types of holding companies which would be regarded as preventing free and fair competition among companies would be banned.

They are extremely large corporate groups whose total assets exceed about 15 trillion yen, corporate groups headed by a large financial institution and groups formed by major companies in the same or related industries.
The FTC must work out guidelines over the establishment of a holding company before the revised law takes effect in order to prevent an excessive concentration of business strength.

Defining a large financial institution as one with assets totalling more than 15 trillion yen would mean major Japanese banks would only be able to set up a holding company to oversee financial companies, such as brokerages and insurance firms. It could not include nonfinancial firms.
The FTC will seek views from the public about the draft guidelines unveiled on Wednesday before making a final decision on them, the official said.
Separately, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) is working out a bill allowing for the establishment of financial holding firms.
Even after the revised anti-monopoly law takes effect, financial institutions will not be allowed to set up financial holding companies until related financial laws are revised.
The ministry is expected to submit the bill in an extraordinary session of parliament this autumn.

Many big Japanese banks have said they are very interested in financial holding companies, which could enable them to adopt more flexible management by setting different pay scales and shutting down unprofitable operations.

But they said they would focus on tax changes related to holding companies. The government has not yet made a final decision on tax changes that will determine whether companies choose to convert into a holding company structure.
